The opening question addressed the August 20 SEC subpoena for document production related to potential federal securities-law violations; the CEO said the company is fully cooperating, the matter is confidential, and it does not affect current or future operations.

Management framed Celsius as 'back-dooring' the energy category - building from gym/specialty roots into grocery, drug, club (Costco a 10%+ customer) and now convenience, where it remains under-indexed.
Central bull thesis: ~18% Amazon share versus only a ~2% tracked-channel share signals the runway in traditional retail.

Identified ~7.5% gross-margin impact from importing cans internationally plus freight inefficiencies in the two-to-six warehouse 'orbit' transition; pressure expected to persist for 'the next several quarters.'
Management said it is 'over investing' in people, systems and infrastructure - 'we're not building this company for just a few share points.'
DSD network only ~68% built out and 'by no means optimized'; expected to be more optimized in 1H 2022.
Co-packing network expanded from 1 to 4 to 3 and now to 13; warehouses moved from two to six in Q3 2021.
Governance upgrades: auditor moved to Ernst & Young in Q3 2021; Board expanded with additional independent directors (accounting/audit, HR, IR expertise).
Celsius is differentiated as science-backed (six-plus published clinical studies) with a loyal, high-recurring consumer base - the key defense against fragmentation risk like hard seltzer.
The hard-seltzer slowdown freed AB-distributor mindshare and focus for Celsius; 'the brand that rotates wins.'
Convenience (~37% ACV) is the biggest distribution opportunity; new doors expected from spring 2022 resets.
Long US can contracts secured for 2022; transient import-cost margin pressure expected to ease over several quarters.

International: launched on Amazon in the UK and Germany, building on a 9%+ Swedish energy share; asset-light master-distributor model invoicing in USD limits FX/AR exposure; North America remains the priority.
Category pricing: everyone effectively taking price via promotional optimization (~4-9% scan increase); Celsius will not lead on frontline pricing.
A 35% long-term EBITDA margin (like Monster) viewed as plausible upon ultimate scale, with in-house raw materials/manufacturing as a future lever; no formal guidance given.
What can management tell investors about the August 20 SEC subpoena for document production related to potential federal securities-law violations?

Confirmed receipt of a general-inquiry subpoena; the company is fully cooperating, the matter is confidential so specifics cannot be discussed, and resolution is expected fairly quickly. Emphasized it does not affect current or future operations.
Can management box in or level-set the geography, timing or materiality of the subpoena?

General inquiries cover a variety of questions; the SEC requested confidentiality, and the company is only required to disclose receipt. Could not say more, but reiterated confidence in current operations and future opportunities.
How has the energy category evolved, and what is the uniqueness of Celsius and its 'right to win'?

A decade dominated by two incumbents is now being disrupted by the better-for-you, functional trend; Celsius offers seven essential vitamins, a fitness/healthy-lifestyle core, and universal appeal across genders, helping it go mainstream from gym/specialty roots. CFO added the current environment magnifies health trends.
Does performance energy risk fragmenting like hard seltzer with large competitors rushing in, and how does Celsius stay differentiated?

The energy category has always absorbed new entrants and has been hard to dominate, unlike the more promotion-driven hard-seltzer category. Celsius's loyal, high-recurring consumer base is the key differentiator; COVID-era Amazon ordering (waiting, chilling, consuming) demonstrated genuine brand loyalty.
How are the Board and organization managing the risk of rapid growth across capacity, human capital, financial capital, distribution and systems?

A balanced, invest-along-the-journey approach: 60 hires in 60 days, 60 open roles, operational transformation (new logistics/production/inventory departments, two-to-six warehouse expansion, co-packers from 1 to 4 to 3 to 13), an Ernst & Young auditor upgrade, an ESG platform, and an expanded Board with more independents.
Does management have the systems and visibility (sales, distributor inventory) to run the business with precision, and how does it perform versus internal plan?

Demand planning and constant forecasting; ~$122M inventory ($80M finished goods) built for the orbit model; raw-material redundancy in cans/flavors; US can contracts for 2022. KPI monitoring (credit limits by DSO, forward-looking inventory, safety stock). Sales/distribution management team (72) targeted above 100 by year-end with new CRM systems.
Update on the DSD transition - how many accounts moved to DSD and the ultimate target?

~68% of stores now serviced by DSD with substantial remaining conversion opportunity, expected optimization in 1H 2022. DSD drives exponentially higher velocity via better in-stock rates, placement and cold positioning - 'if you are cold, you are sold.'
Where is ACV now, when does the convenience ACV gap close, and can velocity surpass incumbents?

Total ACV just under 50%, with convenience the lowest-indexed at ~37% and the biggest opportunity. Celsius is 'back-dooring' the category from gyms/specialty into grocery, drug and Costco, now attacking convenience where the DSD's 'white glove' muscle is essential. The ~18% Amazon share versus ~2% tracked-channel share signals the runway.
Is it reasonable to expect Celsius to replicate Bang's growth - from a 2% share to 7-8% in tracked channels over the next 12-24 months?

Declined to provide forward guidance or 'put a line in the sand' on 24 months, but noted Celsius moved from a 1% to 2% share fairly quickly, sees a massive opportunity, and is 'over investing.' CFO said DSD network leverage should produce a 'snowball effect.'
How did Celsius build such strong Amazon momentum (~20% share, #2), and what is the broader online strategy?

Most fascinating aspect: Amazon share kept growing even as store count more than doubled. With everything 'one click away,' Celsius aims to be wherever the consumer purchases - Amazon, Walmart, shopping apps, Instacart. 'Nothing special' about the strategy beyond brand resonance.
Was management surprised by the velocity improvement from switching to DSD?

DSD does not work for every brand - many revert to wholesale due to insufficient velocity - but Celsius performs extremely well (429% Q3 DSD growth). DSD networks move high volumes (pallets, truckloads), making Celsius a 'perfect alignment'; as an independent brand, it must out-rotate competition to earn distributor attention.
Is the hard-seltzer slowdown fortuitous, freeing AB-distributor mindshare and focus for Celsius?

Agreed - distributors are adding more non-alcoholic products to make up for seltzer's slowdown, creating competition but also more NA focus, and 'the brand that rotates wins.' Celsius is complementary to premium water/hydration offerings, making it incremental.
Comment on the current supply-chain situation and expectations over the next 12 months, given the Q3 inventory build.

Importing cans internationally raises cost versus domestic; going forward depends on the mix of how cans cycle in. CFO said as imported cans flow through the system, the margin impact would persist for 'the next several quarters.'
If Celsius scales to a $1B run-rate, where do EBITDA margins go - and is anything structural preventing a 35% EBITDA margin like Monster?

While noting no formal forward guidance, a 35% margin upon ultimate scale is plausible and Celsius could follow a similar path to Monster, with timing/sequencing key - including bringing some raw materials and manufacturing in-house. Quantified the current ~7.5% margin impact from can imports and six-orbit freight inefficiency.
Given multi-year-high commodity inflation and Monster/Red Bull not moving on price, what will the incumbents do and how does pricing play out?

Everyone is effectively taking price - average retail scans up ~4-9% via promotional optimization - even if no one raises frontline list prices. Celsius has aggressively optimized its promotional strategy and sees further leverage as a premium offering, but will not lead on frontline pricing; has 'no control' over the incumbents.
Comment on the under-appreciated international potential and what is needed distribution-wise to get the international business going.

Cited a 9%+ Swedish energy share, further Norway/Finland distribution, and new Amazon launches in the UK and Germany - the global opportunity is 'huge' with universal health-and-wellness trends, including Asia, South Korea and Australia. CFO stressed an asset-light go-to-market via USD-invoiced master distributors to limit legal-entity, inventory and AR risk; North America remains the priority focus.
